##Problem 1

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)

library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

glimpse(ny_noaa)
```
```{r data-summary}
#To view the number of weather stasions & date rage
station_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    n_stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(station_summary)

missing_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    #view the number of the missing value in every column
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) %>%
  #Change the data missing-value table form horizonal to vertical
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_n"
  ) %>%
  #Calculate the missing percentage for each variable
  mutate(
    missing_percent = 100 * missing_n / nrow(ny_noaa)
  )

missing_summary

```
The NY NOAA dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables from 747 weather stations in New York State, covering from January 1, 1981, through December 31, 2010. Each row represents a daily weather record for one station. The variables include station ID (`id`), observation date(`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

There are no missing values in `id` or `date`. However, 5.62% of precipitation values, 14.69% of snowfall values, and 22.80% of snow depth values are missing. Both maximum and minimum temperature have about 43.71% missing values. Missing data are therefore a substantial issue, like for temperature analyses. And it could affect comparisons across stations and years if missingness varies between these groups.

```{r cleaning}
#Cleaning data
noaa_clean = ny_noaa %>%
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    prcp = prcp/10
  )

glimpse(noaa_clean)
summary(
  select(noaa_clean, tmax, tmin, prcp, snow, snwd)
)

```
```{r snowfall}
snowfall_counts = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(snow)) %>%
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

snowfall_counts
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm. Because many days have no snowfall.


```{r monthly-temperature, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Average maximum temperatures in January and July
monthly_temp = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    month %in% c(1, 7),
    !is.na(tmax)
  ) %>%
  group_by(id, year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    n_days = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  monthly_temp,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "blue", size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station and year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

July is much warmer than January, and January shows larger changes across years. Many stations follow similar patterns, with some years being warmer or colder than others. For example, January 2003 looks especially cold.

There are also a few possible outliers. One station has an unusually low July average of about 14°C around 1988.


```{r temperature-relationship, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
#Temperature relationship & snowfall distribution
temperature_plot = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax),
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 70) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    transform = "log10",
    name = "Count"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum versus minimum temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

temperature_plot

```

```{r snowfall-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year
snowfall_plot = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "green",
    outlier.size = 0.5,
    outlier.alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    subtitle = "Daily snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
  )

snowfall_plot
```


```{r combined-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
library(patchwork)

combined_plot = (temperature_plot / snowfall_plot) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

combined_plot
```
Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship with a few unusual observations away from the main pattern.

Snowfall distributions are fairly similar across years, with medians around 25 mm. Some years, such as 2006, have a smaller interquartile range. There is no clear long-term trend among daily snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 mm.


##Problem 2
```{r import-nhanes}
#Import data
covar_raw = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

accel_raw = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(covar_raw)

dim(accel_raw)

accel_raw %>%
  select(SEQN, min1:min5) %>%
  head()
```


```{r clean-covariates}
#clean data
covar_clean = covar_raw %>%
  rename(
    seqn = SEQN,
    bmi = BMI
  ) %>%
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) %>%
  filter(age >= 21) %>%
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

glimpse(covar_clean)

covar_clean %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    min_age = min(age),
    max_age = max(age),
    missing_values = sum(is.na(pick(everything())))
  )
```


```{r merge-nhanes}
#Tidy and merge activity data
accel_long = accel_raw %>%
  rename(seqn = SEQN) %>%
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "mims"
  )

nhanes = covar_clean %>%
  left_join(accel_long, by = "seqn")

glimpse(nhanes)

nhanes %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n_distinct(seqn),
    n_rows = n(),
    n_minutes = n_distinct(minute),
    missing_mims = sum(is.na(mims))
  )
```

```{r education-table}
participant_df = nhanes %>%
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education)

education_table = participant_df %>%
  count(education, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  arrange(education)

knitr::kable(
  education_table,
  col.names = c("Education level", "Men", "Women"),
  caption = "Number of participants by education level and sex"
)
```


```{r age-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#age distributions by education and sex
ggplot(
  participant_df,
  aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 1.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by education level and sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The more-than-high-school group is the largest, with 56 men and 59 women, and generally has younger participants. The high-school-
equivalent group includes more men than women, but women have a higher median age. In the less-than-high-school group, the numbers of men and women are nearly equal, and their age distributions are similar. Ages vary widely within all groups.


```{r total-activity, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Total activity and age
activity_total = nhanes %>%
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) %>%
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  activity_total,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity(MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all education groups, although the trends are not strictly linear. Women tend to have higher activity levels than men in the high-school-equivalent and more-than-high-school groups. Sex differences are less consistent in the less-than-high-school group. Activity levels also vary widely among participants of similar ages.

```{r daily-activity-pattern, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Activity patterns over 24 hours
activity_by_minute = nhanes %>%
  group_by(education, sex, minute) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(hour = (minute - 1) / 60)

ggplot(
  activity_by_minute,
  aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    span = 0.15,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Activity patterns over 24 hours",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

All three education groups show low activity overnight, a sharp rise in the morning, and a decline in the evening. The less-than-high-school group has a clear peak around noon, with similar daytime patterns for men and women. Women generally have higher daytime activity than men in the other two groups, especially in the more-than-high-school group.

##Problem 3
```{r check-citibike-files}
#impoort data
list.files("data/citibike")
```

```{r import-citibike}
jan_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july_2020 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july_2024 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(year = 2024, month ="July")

citibike_raw = bind_rows(
  jan_2020, july_2020, jan_2024, july_2024
)

glimpse(citibike_raw)

citibike_raw %>%
  count(year, month)
```


```{r check-citibike-data}
#to check data quality in order to clean
citibike_raw %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_values"
  )

citibike_raw %>%
  summarise(
    duplicate_ids = n() - n_distinct(ride_id),
    min_duration = min(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_duration = max(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    nonpositive_duration = sum(duration <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

citibike_raw %>%
  count(rideable_type, member_casual)
```


```{r clean-citibike}
#to clean the data
citibike = citibike_raw %>%
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2020, 2024)),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday","Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic bike", "Electric bike")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual","member"),
      labels = c("Casual","Member")
    )
  )
glimpse(citibike)
citibike %>%
  summarise(
    n_rides = n(),
    n_variables = ncol(citibike),
    missing_start = sum(is.na(start_station_name)),
    missing_end = sum(is.na(end_station_name))
  )
```
The dataset contains 99,485 rides and 9 variables from January and July of 2020 and 2024. Each row represents one ride, with information： ride ID, bike type, day of the week, duration in minutes, starting and ending stations, membership status, year, and month. Starting station names are missing for 43 rides. Ending station names are missing for 207 rides.


```{r citibike-ride-count}
#to show the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members
ride_counts = citibike %>%
  count(year, month, member_casual) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  arrange(year, month)

knitr::kable(
  ride_counts,
  col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual riders", "Members"),
  caption = "Number of rides in the sample by year, month, and membership", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)
```
Members account for most rides in all four months. Both casual and member rides are more common in July than in January and increased from 2020 to 2024. July 2024 has the most rides, with 10,894 casual rides and 36,262 member rides.

### Most popular starting stations in July 2024

```{r top-starting-stations}
#showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024
top_stations = citibike %>%
  filter(
    year == "2024",
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) %>%
  count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_rides), start_station_name) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

knitr::kable(
  top_stations,
  col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"),
  caption = "Five most popular starting stations in the July 2024 sample",format.args = list(big.mark = ",")
)
```


```{r median-ride-duration, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
median_duration = citibike %>%
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) %>%
  summarise( median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  median_duration,
  aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = month,
    group = month
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("January" = "blue", "July" = "green")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday, month and year",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

Median ride duration is higher in July than in January on every day in both years, and is lower in 2024 than in 2020. Weekend rides are longer in 2020 and in July 2024, while January 2024 shows little variation across the week. The highest median duration is about 16.5 minutes on weekends in July 2020.


```{r duration-distribution-2024, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
#Ride duration distributions in 2024
citibike_2024 = citibike %>%
  filter(year == "2024")

ggplot(
  citibike_2024,
  aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    outlier.alpha = 0.1,
    outlier.size = 0.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~month, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Classic bike" = "blue",
      "Electric bike" = "pink"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration distributions in 2024",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes, log)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Casual riders generally take longer rides than members in both months. Median ride durations are higher in July than in January across all groups. Among casual riders, classic bike rides tend to be longer than electric bike rides.For members, durations are similar between bike types in January, while electric bike rides tend to be longer in July. All groups include some unusually long rides.
